newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French troops drawn into Central African flare-up.
newsitem.headline: French troops drawn into Central African flare-up.

text.p: French troops were on Sunday drawn into fighting between disaffected soldiers and peacekeepers in the Central African Republic that has so far left around 30 people dead.
A French general told French television that the troops intervened in the capital Bangui to stop the Central African soldiers from attacking the peacekeepers.

"As part of support for the African force, French forces in Bangui became involved as part of self-defence to stop firing at Senegalese and Chadian positions," General Jean-Pierre Perez told La Chaine Info.

Perez, the commander of French troops stationed in Bangui, said the Central African ex-mutineers had started firing mortars at Chadian and Senegalese positions on Sunday afternoon after a lull earlier in the day.
He did not say how many French troops were involved in the action in the former colony nor whether there were any casualties. Some reports in Bangui spoke of a French soldier being among the injured.
Witnesses also said French helicopters were flying over the city.
Officials of the Central African Red Cross said the death toll after three days of fighting between former mutineers and peacekeepers had risen to around 30. Around 70 people have been wounded.
The injured in the fighting include five French nationals, who were hit on Saturday by two stray mortar bombs that fell on the French embassy compound.
The African peacekeeping force has been deployed since a January 25 peace deal that ended a series of mutinies.

That deal, brokered by Mali's respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure, included a plan to reintegrate the mutineers from the paramilitary gendarmerie into their units, but efforts to achieve this have failed.
Toure was expected in Bangui to intervene again on Sunday, but officials could not say whether he had arrived.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
French troops -- there are 1,650 stationed in the country as part of a bilateral defence accord -- restored order after the last mutiny and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
The African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier was among the first casualties of the flare-up on Friday.
